items.bodyEn: Fuchū was the castle town of Sunpu, where Tokugawa Ieyasu spent his last years, 1607 to 1616. West of town the Abe River had no bridge or ferry: licensed porters carried travellers over on their shoulders or on a shared platform, with fares set by the day's water depth. Hiroshige's 'Fuchū: The Abe River' shows exactly that crossing.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, 'Fuchū: The Abe River' (Hōeidō ed.); Tōkaidō Meisho Zue (1797)

items.bodyEn: Fuchū means 'in the provincial seat': every old province had a kokufu, so Japan still has several Fuchūs. Suruga's was renamed in 1869; the usual explanation is that fuchū sounded like the fuchū meaning 'disloyal', awkward under a new government. Shizuoka, 'quiet hill', was taken from Shizuhata-yama behind the castle, with its unflattering first kanji, 'lowly', swapped for 'quiet'.
items.ja: {府中|ふちゅう}・{不忠|ふちゅう}
items.sourceNote: Kōjien, entries 府中・国府; Shizuoka city histories on the 1869 renaming

items.bodyEn: そうだ changes meaning with what it attaches to. On the ます-stem it reports what you see: ふりそうだ, 'it looks like rain'; たかそう, 'looks expensive'; いい becomes よさそう. On a plain form it reports what you heard: ふるそうだ, 'I hear it will rain'; たかいそうだ, 'they say it's expensive'. Same three kana, so check the verb ending before you decide.
items.ja: {降|ふ}りそうだ。{降|ふ}るそうだ。
items.kana: ふりそうだ。ふるそうだ。

items.titleEn: Rain or candy: ame and ame
items.bodyEn: Rain set the porters’ fare at the Abe, so learn the word. In Tokyo pitch, 雨 rain is A-me: high on a, drop on me, and the particle stays low: A-me-ga. 飴 candy is a-ME: low then high, with no drop, so the particle stays high: a-ME-GA. One mora decides whether you are offered a sweet or a storm.
